t-4438.author: kwame.a
t-4438.title: Docker: container cannot reach another container by name on the default bridge network
t-4438.body: Two containers started with plain `docker run`. From `app` I do `curl db:5432` and get "Could not resolve host: db". Both show up in `docker ps`. Linking is deprecated so I have not used it. What am I missing?

replies.author: kwame.a
replies.body:
Answering my own question after finding it. The default `bridge` network does not provide DNS between containers; only user-defined networks do. Create one and attach both containers:

docker network create backend
docker run -d --name db --network backend postgres:16
docker run -d --name app --network backend myapp

Now `db` resolves from `app`. Docker Compose does this for you, which is why the same setup works there and not with bare `docker run`.

t-4452.author: tvu
t-4452.title: Bash: my script breaks on file names with spaces
t-4452.body:
for f in $(ls *.log); do
  gzip $f
done

Fails on `server 2026-09.log`. I know I should quote things but I do not know which things.

replies.author: dmorel
replies.body:
Quote every expansion, and do not parse `ls`. The shell glob already gives you a list with each name as one word:

for f in *.log; do
  gzip -- "$f"
done

`$(ls *.log)` turns the output back into text and splits it on whitespace, which is where the space in the name becomes two arguments. The double quotes around `"$f"` keep it one argument on the way into gzip. `--` protects you from a file named `-r`. Run scripts through shellcheck; it flags exactly this.

comments.author: tvu
comments.body: shellcheck flagged four other lines while I was at it.

replies.author: s-kovac
replies.body: For recursive cases use `find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 gzip`, where the NUL separator makes any file name safe, including ones with newlines.

t-4456.author: rgoyal
t-4456.title: pandas: groupby then keep the row with the maximum value per group
t-4456.body: df has columns user, ts, score. I want, for each user, the whole row where score is highest. `df.groupby('user').max()` gives me the max of every column independently, which mixes rows.

replies.author: rgoyal
replies.body:
Two idiomatic ways. With `idxmax`, which returns the index label of the max per group and then selects those rows:

best = df.loc[df.groupby('user')['score'].idxmax()]

Or sort and drop duplicates, which is faster on wide frames:

best = df.sort_values('score', ascending=False).drop_duplicates('user')

Both keep whole rows. `groupby().max()` is column-wise by design, which is why it mixed them.

replies.author: jlindqvist
replies.body: If there can be ties and you want all tied rows, use `df[df.score == df.groupby('user').score.transform('max')]`.

t-4470.author: dev_nadia
t-4470.title: CORS error calling my API from localhost:3000, but curl works
t-4470.body:
Access to fetch at api.local:8080/users from origin localhost:3000 has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present.

curl returns the JSON fine. Is the browser broken?

replies.author: hgroth
replies.body:
The browser is doing its job. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server, which is why curl - which has no origin - is unaffected. Your API needs to tell the browser that the page's origin is allowed, by answering with:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <the page's origin, e.g. localhost:3000>

and, for requests with custom headers or JSON bodies, answering the OPTIONS preflight with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. Most frameworks have a middleware for it; set the allowed origin explicitly rather than `*` if you also send cookies, because `*` is refused with credentials. For local development, a dev-server proxy that makes the API same-origin avoids the whole thing.

comments.author: dev_nadia
comments.body: Added the middleware and the preflight started returning 204. Working now.

t-4481.author: dev_nadia
t-4481.title: Python: mutable default argument keeps growing between calls
t-4481.body:
def add(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

add(1) -> [1]
add(2) -> [1, 2]  ??

I expected a fresh list each call.

replies.author: jlindqvist
replies.body:
Default values are evaluated once, when the `def` runs, not each call. The same list object is shared by every call that does not pass its own. The idiom is a sentinel:

def add(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

Linters flag this as B006. The same applies to dicts, sets and any other mutable default.
